executive_summary: The most important connecting thread across today's content is the contested terrain of institutional power and who gets to wield it — a theme that runs from The Atlantic's in-depth analysis of masculinism to Foreign Affairs' coverage of Orban's fall and Europe's political realignment. The Atlantic's piece frames masculinism not as an organic response to male grievance but as a deliberately engineered right-wing political project designed to consolidate power by rolling back women's legal and professional standing, making it fundamentally a story about institutional control masquerading as cultural grievance. Foreign Affairs echoes this dynamic on the geopolitical stage, where Orban's weakening grip and the accompanying shifts in European power structures reveal how authoritarian consolidation — whether domestic or transnational — carries the seeds of its own fragility. Together, these pieces argue, implicitly but forcefully, that movements built on the reversal of others' rights rather than the construction of genuine coalitions are ultimately unstable political projects. This thread matters because it reframes several seemingly disparate stories — gender politics, European democracy, and even the Musk-OpenAI legal battle over who controls transformative technology — as variations on the same question: who holds institutional power, and how far will they go to keep it.

That was Victor Wembanyama's stat line from the Spurs' 122-115 double-overtime victory in Game 1 of the Western Conference finals last night. Since blocked shots started being recorded in the 1973-74 season, only three players have put up 40 points, 24 boards and three blocks in a playoff game. newsletters.title: Here’s why Elon Musk lost his suit against OpenAI

items.headline: Here's why Elon Musk lost his suit against OpenAI
items.blurb:
Elon Musk has lost his lawsuit against OpenAI, which centered on whether the company breached its founding contract as a nonprofit. A jury found that he sued too late, meaning his claims are barred by statutes of limitations. But the verdict didn't judge if OpenAI violated its nonprofit mission—only whether Musk brought the case in time.

The dispute hinged on when OpenAI began shifting toward a for-profit structure. The company argued that signs of a shift were visible as early as 2017, while Musk said he only discovered the change in 2022.

items.headline: Inside Anduril and Meta's quest to make smart glasses for warfare
items.blurb:
The defense-tech company Anduril has shared new details about the augmented-reality headset for the military it's prototyping with Meta, including a vision for ordering drone strikes via eye-tracking and voice commands.

Quay Barnett, who leads the effort at Anduril following a career in the Army's Special Operations Command, says he aims to optimize "the human as a weapons system."

items.headline: What to expect at Google I/O this week
items.blurb:
When Google opens its doors today for its annual developer conference, I/O, it will do so as a clear third place in the foundation model race.

A foundation model's reputation these days rests largely on its coding capabilities, and for months Google's coding tools have been outgunned by Anthropic's Claude Code and OpenAI's Codex. But the company still shapes the cutting edge in areas such as AI for science. At I/O this week, it will try to prove it can compete on both fronts.

items.headline: Can AI learn to understand the world?
items.blurb:
As the limits of LLMs become clearer, researchers are developing a new kind of AI designed to understand the physical environment: world models.

Recent developments from Google DeepMind, Fei-Fei Li's World Labs, and Yann LeCun's new startup have pushed these systems to the forefront of AI. At an upcoming virtual event, MIT Technology Review will examine the progress—and what comes next.

longform.title: Why I don’t buy masculinism
longform.thesis: Masculinism — a coordinated right-wing movement seeking to reverse women's legal, professional, and political gains — is best understood not as a legitimate response to male struggle but as a misogynist project whose primary political function is to unify the American right.
longform.context: The piece is a pre-publication author's note from Helen Lewis accompanying her June 2026 Atlantic cover story, written in response to the rising visibility of self-described masculinists in conservative politics, several of whom have proximity to figures like Pete Hegseth in the current political moment.
arguments: Masculinism's policy agenda is explicitly restorationist and radical: its proponents advocate repealing the Nineteenth Amendment, instituting a 'family wage' to push women out of the workforce, and reversing the 'great feminization' of professional life — positions Lewis frames not as fringe but as held by 'high-profile thinkers on the right.'

The movement's leading figures — pastor Douglas Wilson, online personality Raw Egg Nationalist, and essayist Helen Andrews — advance pseudo-biological and theological claims (low testosterone causes liberalism; female authority is 'a threat to civilization') that Lewis treats as intellectually weak but politically potent, requiring serious engagement rather than dismissal.

Lewis distinguishes genuine male disadvantage (e.g., men comprising the majority of problem gamblers) from the masculinist diagnosis, rejecting the core claim that 'feminism has ruined America' and that women secretly want patriarchy restored — a distinction she frames as the analytic crux of her investigation.

The masculinists' shared target — empathy, characterized as 'dangerous, feminine softness toward immigrants and criminals' — reveals that the movement's coherence is ideological and tactical, serving as a binding agent for the contemporary American right rather than a response to any empirical crisis of masculinity.
longform.significance: The piece matters because it situates a diffuse online misogyny within formal conservative politics at a moment of Republican governance, arguing this is 'the single most important force holding together the American right' — a claim that reframes gender politics as a structural feature of the current coalition, not a cultural sideshow. It also models an analytical problem: how to take male disadvantage seriously without legitimizing a movement that exploits it.
questions_raised: Lewis acknowledges that some men and boys are genuinely struggling in under-examined ways — but the brief does not resolve how policymakers or journalists should address those real issues without providing rhetorical ammunition to masculinists who weaponize the same data.

If masculinism functions primarily as political glue for the right rather than as a coherent ideology, what would actually dislodge it — and does Lewis's critique risk amplifying a movement whose power depends on elite attention?
